First Home Buyer

First Home Buyer Australia 2026: The Complete Guide From Saving to Settlement

Published: 2 May 2026 · Last updated: 4 June 2026 · By Emma Hartley, CFP

Buying your first home in Australia in 2026 is genuinely achievable — but it requires more planning than most people expect. The median Australian home price crossed $1 million nationally in 2026. That sounds daunting, but government support has also expanded significantly. The First Home Guarantee now has no income caps and unlimited places, Help to Buy launched in December 2025 as a new shared equity scheme, and state grants in Queensland reach $30,000 for new builds. With the right strategy, many first home buyers can enter the market with as little as 5% deposit — without paying Lenders Mortgage Insurance (LMI).

How Much Do You Actually Need to Save?

This is the question almost every first home buyer gets wrong. The deposit is not the only cash you need. Many buyers hit their deposit target and then discover at settlement that they are short because they forgot to budget for stamp duty, legal fees, building inspections, and lender charges. A rough rule is to add 5–8% on top of your deposit target to cover all upfront costs.

The standard deposit benchmark is 20% of the purchase price. At 20%, your loan-to-value ratio sits at 80%, which means you avoid LMI — a one-off insurance premium that protects the lender (not you) if you default. On a $700,000 purchase, LMI can cost $17,000–$25,000. That said, government schemes now allow eligible first home buyers to purchase with a 5% or even 2% deposit without triggering LMI at all.

For a $700,000 purchase, here is a realistic breakdown of total upfront costs across four states in 2026, assuming a 5% deposit and first home buyer concessions apply:

State 5% Deposit Stamp Duty (FHB) Conveyancing Inspection Total Cash (approx.)
NSW $35,000 $0 (waived under $800K) $1,600 $600 ~$37,200
VIC $35,000 ~$0–$8,800 (waived under $600K; concession to $750K) $1,500 $600 ~$37,100–$46,000
QLD $35,000 $0 (waived under $700K) $1,200 $550 ~$36,750
WA $35,000 $0 (waived under $450K; partial concession to $600K) $1,800 $550 ~$37,350+

Always verify current stamp duty thresholds at your state's revenue office, as these figures can change. Every First Home Buyer Scheme Available in 2026

Australia's landscape of first home buyer support changed substantially in late 2025. Here is a clear breakdown of every federal scheme currently active.

First Home Guarantee — 5% Deposit, No LMI

The First Home Guarantee — administered by Housing Australia — allows eligible first home buyers to purchase with a 5% deposit without paying LMI. The federal government guarantees up to 15% of the loan to the lender, so you still own 100% of your home from day one.

The scheme was significantly expanded from 1 October 2025. Income caps (previously $125,000 for singles, $200,000 for couples) have been removed entirely. There are now unlimited places — no more annual waitlists or place limits. Property price caps have also been lifted, with Sydney's cap now at $1,500,000, Melbourne at $950,000, and Brisbane at $1,000,000.

You apply through a participating lender — you cannot apply directly to Housing Australia. The panel of approved lenders includes major banks such as CBA, NAB, and Westpac, as well as a range of smaller banks and non-bank lenders.

Family Home Guarantee — 2% Deposit for Single Parents

Single parents or single legal guardians with at least one dependent child can purchase with a 2% deposit and no LMI under the Family Home Guarantee. The government guarantees up to 18% of the loan value. An income cap of $125,000 applies. This scheme recognises that single-income households face fundamentally different savings challenges.

Help to Buy — New Shared Equity Scheme, Launched December 2025

Help to Buy is Australia's brand new federal shared equity scheme. Under this model, the government co-purchases the property with you, contributing up to 40% of the purchase price for new builds and up to 30% for existing homes. In return, the government holds an equivalent equity stake. When you sell or refinance, you repay the government's proportionate share — including any capital growth.

You can enter with just a 2% deposit and a significantly smaller loan. Income caps apply: singles must earn under $100,000 per year and couples under $160,000 combined. There are 10,000 places per year, allocated on a first-come, first-served basis. This scheme is ideal for lower-income buyers who want the smallest possible monthly repayment. The trade-off is clear: you share any future property gains with the government. It cannot be combined with the First Home Guarantee — you must choose one.

First Home Super Saver (FHSS) Scheme

The FHSS scheme allows you to make voluntary contributions to your superannuation fund and later withdraw them — plus associated earnings — for your first home deposit. You can contribute up to $15,000 per financial year and withdraw up to $50,000 in total. For couples, this doubles to $100,000 combined.

The tax advantage is meaningful. Concessional (before-tax) contributions into super are taxed at just 15%, which is typically far below your marginal income tax rate. On a $90,000 salary, saving $15,000 a year through the FHSS scheme saves approximately $5,000–$7,000 in tax compared with saving in a standard bank account — every single year you contribute.

There are important timing rules. You must obtain an FHSS determination from the ATO before signing your property contract. The release request then takes 15–25 business days to process. You only get one FHSS release in your lifetime, so plan carefully. The FHSS can be combined with the First Home Guarantee, meaning you can build your deposit inside super tax-effectively, then use it alongside the 5% deposit guarantee when you are ready to buy.

State-Based Grants (First Home Owner Grant)

Most states offer a First Home Owner Grant (FHOG) for new or substantially renovated properties. Note that state grants generally apply only to new homes or substantial renovations, not established properties. Stamp duty concessions, however, often cover both new and existing properties depending on the state.

State FHOG Amount Property Cap
NSW $10,000 New homes ≤$600,000 (or land + build ≤$750,000)
VIC $10,000 (regional areas) New homes ≤$750,000
QLD $30,000 New homes ≤$750,000 (until 30 June 2026)
WA $10,000 New homes ≤$750,000
TAS Grant available Check sro.tas.gov.au for current eligibility

How to Save Your Deposit Faster

Use the FHSS scheme from day one. If you are more than 12 months from buying, start making voluntary super contributions now. Every dollar you contribute saves you tax on the way in. The sooner you start, the larger your tax saving.

Open a high-interest savings account. As of mid-2026, the top savings rates in Australia are between 5.0% and 5.5% per annum. On a $50,000 balance, that generates $2,500–$2,750 per year in interest — meaningful progress toward your target.

Run a 50/30/20 budget. Allocate 50% of take-home income to essentials, 30% to discretionary spending, and 20% or more directly to your deposit savings account. Use our Budget Calculator to map your current spending against the 50/30/20 framework and identify where you can redirect more toward savings.

Reduce your taxable income legally. Salary sacrificing additional amounts into superannuation lowers your taxable income, which means lower PAYG withholding from your employer and more after-tax cash. See our Salary Sacrifice Calculator to model the exact dollar saving.

Know your savings timeline. Use our Savings Goal Calculator to enter your target amount, current balance, monthly savings, and interest rate — and get a clear month-by-month projection.

Getting Pre-Approval: What Lenders Actually Check

Pre-approval is a written confirmation from a lender of how much they are prepared to lend you, subject to final property and income verification. It is not a guaranteed loan offer — but it is an essential tool before you start house-hunting.

To assess your pre-approval, lenders evaluate your gross income, regular living expenses, any existing debts (including HECS-HELP balances, which reduce borrowing capacity), credit card limits, employment stability, and credit score. You will typically need to provide your last three payslips, three to six months of bank statements, identification documents, and statements for all existing financial commitments.

Pre-approval typically remains valid for 90 days. Critically, do not make any significant financial changes during this period. Taking out a new car loan, applying for additional credit cards, or changing jobs can invalidate your pre-approval — even after you have exchanged contracts.

One important note on HECS-HELP debt: lenders assess HECS repayments as a monthly obligation. A $50,000 HECS balance can reduce your borrowing capacity by $30,000–$50,000 depending on the lender. Use our HECS Repayment Calculator to understand your current annual repayment and how it affects your financial position.

The Buying Process: Private Treaty vs Auction

Buying via Private Treaty

The vendor sets an asking price. You make an offer and negotiate until both parties agree. Once the vendor accepts, you exchange contracts. In most states, a cooling-off period applies: 5 business days in NSW and QLD, 3 days in Victoria. During cooling-off, you can withdraw from the purchase, though a small penalty (typically 0.25% of the purchase price) may apply. Use this window to complete your building and pest inspection and have your solicitor review the contract. Once the cooling-off period expires and any conditions are met, the contract becomes unconditional and settlement is scheduled — usually 30–90 days after exchange.

Buying at Auction

At auction, there is no cooling-off period. If you are the highest bidder and the property sells above the reserve price, you are immediately and unconditionally committed to the purchase. You sign the contract on the day and pay the deposit — typically 10% — on the spot. This means all your due diligence must be completed before the auction: unconditional pre-approval, a reviewed contract, and a completed building and pest inspection. Never bid at auction without having done all three. A failed settlement after a successful auction bid can result in forfeiting your entire 10% deposit.

Settlement: What Happens on the Day

Settlement is the legal transfer of property ownership from the vendor to you. Your conveyancer coordinates the exchange of funds and title documents with the vendor's conveyancer. In 2026, almost all Australian settlements are conducted electronically through the PEXA platform.

On settlement day, your lender releases the loan funds, the vendor's mortgage is discharged, the title is transferred into your name, and your conveyancer confirms completion. After that, the real estate agent releases the keys. Your conveyancer will also conduct a final title search before settlement to confirm there are no outstanding caveats, orders, or encumbrances on the property.

Upfront Costs That First Home Buyers Frequently Miss

Building and pest inspection ($400–$700). Non-negotiable for any established property. A professional inspection identifies structural defects, water damage, termite activity, and safety issues that are not visible to the naked eye. A single missed defect can cost $30,000 or more to rectify.

Conveyancing fees ($900–$2,500). Your conveyancer handles the contract review, title searches, liaising with your lender, and coordinating settlement. The fee varies by state and complexity. Do not try to save money here — a conveyancing error can cost far more than the fee itself.

Lender fees ($0–$700). Many lenders charge an application fee, valuation fee, or settlement fee. Some lenders waive these for first home buyers under government guarantee schemes. Ask explicitly before selecting a lender.

Moving costs ($500–$3,000+). Professional movers for a two-bedroom apartment typically cost $800–$1,500. A four-bedroom house with interstate contents can reach $3,000–$5,000. Budget for this separately.

Immediate repairs or appliances. Even in a well-maintained property, first home buyers commonly spend $2,000–$8,000 in the first three months on items the vendor left behind or wore out before settlement — hot water systems, blinds, appliances, and garden maintenance.

Worked Example: Sophie's Journey From Saving to Settlement

Real numbers make the process far easier to understand. Here is how a typical first home buyer in Brisbane — let's call her Sophie — navigates the entire journey in 2026.

Sophie's starting position. Sophie is 29, earns $88,000 per year as a project coordinator, and has $18,000 in savings. She has a $32,000 HECS-HELP debt. She wants to buy a two-bedroom unit in Brisbane's inner suburbs, targeting a purchase price of $650,000.

Step 1: Setting the savings target

Sophie's 5% deposit on a $650,000 property is $32,500. Queensland waives stamp duty for first home buyers on properties under $700,000, so her stamp duty cost is $0. Adding conveyancing ($1,200), a building inspection ($550), and a small lender fee buffer ($500), her total upfront cash requirement is approximately $34,750. She already has $18,000, meaning she needs to save a further $16,750.

Step 2: Using the FHSS to save tax

Sophie starts salary sacrificing $1,000 per month into her super fund as concessional contributions. At her marginal tax rate of 32.5%, she would normally pay $325 in tax on each $1,000 earned. Inside super, it is taxed at just 15% — saving her $175 per month, or $2,100 per year. Over 14 months, she accumulates $14,000 in eligible FHSS contributions plus associated earnings, bringing her total FHSS release amount to approximately $13,800 after the 30% tax offset on withdrawal. She keeps her remaining savings in a high-interest account earning 5.2% per annum. After 14 months of also depositing $900 per month into savings, she reaches her $34,750 target.

Step 3: Getting pre-approval

Sophie applies for pre-approval through a participating First Home Guarantee lender. The lender calculates her borrowing capacity using her $88,000 income, minus her HECS-HELP repayment obligation of $4,928 per year (5.6% of income above the 2026–27 threshold), and her estimated living expenses. After APRA's 3% serviceability buffer is applied, Sophie receives pre-approval for a maximum loan of $530,000 — enough to comfortably purchase at $650,000 with a 5% deposit.

Step 4: Applying for the First Home Guarantee

Because Sophie is a first home buyer purchasing with a 5% deposit in Brisbane (price cap: $1,000,000), she qualifies for the First Home Guarantee. There are no income caps in 2026, so her $88,000 salary is not a barrier. The government guarantees 15% of her loan — $97,500 — which means she pays zero LMI on the $617,500 loan. At typical LMI rates for her LVR, this saves her approximately $18,000. She also checks Queensland's $30,000 First Home Owner Grant — but the FHOG applies only to new homes, and Sophie is buying an established unit, so she does not qualify. She still benefits from the full stamp duty exemption and the LMI saving.

Step 5: The purchase and settlement

Sophie finds a two-bedroom unit listed at $645,000 via private treaty. She makes an offer of $638,000, which the vendor accepts. Contracts are exchanged with a 5-business-day cooling-off period. Her building inspector identifies minor issues only (cost: $530). Her conveyancer finds no unusual contract conditions. She waives cooling-off and the contract becomes unconditional. Settlement is set for 45 days after exchange. On settlement day, her lender releases the $605,500 loan, the vendor's mortgage is discharged, and title transfers electronically through PEXA. Sophie's conveyancer confirms completion at 2:14 pm. The agent releases the keys an hour later.

Sophie's final cost summary

ItemAmount
Purchase price$638,000
5% deposit (cash)$31,900
FHSS release (applied to deposit)$13,800
Stamp duty$0 (exempted)
Conveyancing$1,200
Building inspection$530
Lender fees$400
Moving costs$900
Total cash out of pocket~$35,930
LMI saved via First Home Guarantee~$18,000
Tax saved via FHSS (over 14 months)~$2,450

Sophie bought a $638,000 property for a total cash outlay of approximately $35,930 — with no LMI, no stamp duty, and a meaningful tax saving from the FHSS scheme. Without these government schemes, her upfront costs would have exceeded $55,000.

The 5 Most Expensive First Home Buyer Mistakes

Bidding at auction without unconditional pre-approval. If your finance falls through after a successful auction bid, you lose your 10% deposit. Always have fully unconditional pre-approval — not just conditional — before you raise your hand.

Buying just over a stamp duty threshold. In Victoria, purchasing at $601,000 instead of $599,000 triggers a concession rather than a full exemption — costing up to $31,000 in additional stamp duty. Check the exact thresholds for your state before setting your maximum budget.

Missing the FHSS timing requirement. You must obtain an FHSS determination from the ATO before signing your property contract. The release request takes 15–25 business days. Many buyers forget this and miss the scheme entirely.

Skipping the building inspection. It is legal to purchase a property without a building inspection. It is also potentially catastrophic. Never skip it — even for a brand-new apartment in a strata scheme.

Maxing out your borrowing capacity with no buffer. Borrowing the maximum your lender will offer leaves you exposed to rate rises, job changes, or unexpected expenses. A buffer of at least three to six months of mortgage repayments in a savings or offset account is the minimum safety margin worth maintaining. See our Offset Account Calculator to see how an offset account reduces your interest.

How to Use This Guide: Your Step-by-Step Action Plan

Reading about buying a home and actually moving through the process are two different things. Here is a practical sequence of actions you can take right now, in order, regardless of where you are in your savings journey.

  1. Know your numbers before anything else. Use CalcPhi's First Home Buyer Calculator to model your stamp duty, upfront costs, and deposit requirements for your target price and state. This gives you a single concrete savings target. Do this today — it takes two minutes.
  2. Check your borrowing power. Use CalcPhi's Borrowing Power Calculator to understand the maximum loan you qualify for at your current income and expenses, including APRA's 3% serviceability buffer. This tells you the property price range worth saving toward.
  3. Open your FHSS contribution immediately. If you are more than 12 months from purchasing, contact your super fund and start making voluntary concessional contributions now. Use CalcPhi's Salary Sacrifice Calculator to find the right contribution level for your budget.
  4. Open a dedicated high-interest savings account. Keep your deposit savings completely separate from your everyday banking. Set up an automatic transfer on the day your salary lands. Target an account paying 5.0%+ per annum. Use CalcPhi's Savings Goal Calculator to track exactly when you will hit your target.
  5. Check stamp duty thresholds for your target state. Use CalcPhi's Stamp Duty Calculator to understand the exact duty payable and the price cap below which you receive a full exemption. Build this threshold into your maximum purchase price before you start house-hunting.
  6. Get your documents organised early. Lenders request the same set of documents for every pre-approval: three recent payslips, three to six months of bank statements, identification documents, existing loan statements, and HECS balance confirmation. Organising these in advance means you can move quickly when you are ready.
  7. Apply for pre-approval through a First Home Guarantee lender. When your savings are 4–8 weeks from target, apply through a lender on the Housing Australia participating lender panel and confirm your eligibility for the First Home Guarantee. Pre-approval is valid for 90 days — apply when you are genuinely ready to start making offers.
  8. Engage a conveyancer before you exchange contracts. Research and shortlist a conveyancer in your state while you are still saving — so you have a name ready to call the moment you receive an accepted offer or want a pre-auction contract reviewed.
  9. Complete building and pest inspection before committing. For private treaty purchases, do this during the cooling-off period. For auctions, do this before bidding. Never skip it, regardless of how competitive the market feels.
  10. Prepare for settlement costs beyond the deposit. In the final weeks before settlement, confirm you have funds available for conveyancing fees, lender fees, and moving costs. These are paid at or around settlement and are separate from your deposit. Running short at this stage — after exchange — is an avoidable and stressful position to be in.

Frequently Asked Questions

  • Can I use the First Home Guarantee if I earn a high income in 2026?

    Yes. As of 1 October 2025, income caps were removed from the First Home Guarantee entirely. Any Australian citizen or permanent resident purchasing their first home can now apply regardless of income, provided the property is within the applicable price cap for their location. There are also now unlimited places, so there is no waiting for a spot to become available.

  • Can I use my superannuation to help buy my first home?

    Yes, through the First Home Super Saver (FHSS) scheme. You can contribute voluntarily to your super fund — up to $15,000 per financial year — and withdraw a total of up to $50,000 (or $100,000 for couples) for your first home deposit. The tax benefit is significant: concessional contributions are taxed at just 15%, which is often much lower than your marginal income tax rate. You must apply for an FHSS determination from the ATO before signing any property contract, and the release takes 15–25 business days.

  • What is LMI and how do I avoid it?

    Lenders Mortgage Insurance (LMI) is a one-off insurance premium that protects the lender — not you — if you default on a home loan with a deposit below 20%. On a $700,000 property with a 5% deposit, LMI can cost $17,000–$25,000. You can avoid it by saving a 20% deposit, by using the First Home Guarantee (5% deposit, no LMI), by using the Family Home Guarantee if you are a single parent (2% deposit, no LMI), or by meeting certain professional exemptions offered by some lenders.

  • How long does settlement take after exchanging contracts?

    Most Australian property settlements occur 30–90 days after exchange of contracts, though this can be negotiated. A 30-day settlement is relatively fast and requires your lender to move quickly — 45–60 days is more common. If you are buying at auction, the settlement timeframe is typically stated in the contract of sale and is non-negotiable.

  • Do I need a conveyancer or a solicitor?

    Both can handle property settlement. A licensed conveyancer specialises specifically in property transfers — they handle the contract review, title searches, and settlement coordination. A property solicitor does all of this and can also provide legal advice if complications arise. For a straightforward residential purchase, a conveyancer is usually sufficient and often less expensive. For properties with complex title issues, off-the-plan purchases, or unusual contract conditions, a property solicitor adds extra protection.

  • Does HECS-HELP debt affect my ability to get a home loan?

    Yes, it reduces your borrowing capacity. Lenders treat HECS repayments as a monthly expense regardless of your actual income-based repayment. A $50,000 HECS balance can reduce your maximum loan by $30,000–$50,000 depending on the lender's methodology.
